items.title: Trump orders removal of Canadian goods from U.S. federal procurement. Live updates here.
items.description: The latest escalation in the Canada-U.S. trade war comes as Mark Carney meets with foreign leaders in Europe while Pierre Poilievre criticized the prime minister. Follow for live updates.
items._ogDesc: The latest escalation in the Canada-U.S. trade war comes as Mark Carney meets with foreign leaders in Europe while Pierre Poilievre criticized the prime minister. Follow for live updates.
items.body:
In the latest escalation to the Canada-U.S. trade war, ‌Donald Trump has ​signed a presidential ​memorandum to ⁠identify ⁠and remove Canadian-origin goods ‌in U.S. federal ⁠civil government procurement.

Meanwhile Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre called out Prime Minister Mark Carney for “secretly negotiating with the EU and said Canada must remain “independent” amid talk of deepening ties with Europe.

Earlier today, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she wants Canada to become the bloc’s first associate member. But Canada’s ambassador designate says Ottawa is “not there” yet.

Von der Leyen made the remark during her State of the Union address to the EU Parliament Wednesday. Carney will address members tomorrow following a whirlwind trip around Europe.

  • Trump signs memorandum to remove Canadian goods from U.S. procurement
  • Poilievre criticizes Carney during caucus remarks and Conservatives say ‘no EU taxes’
  • Albertans are being cautioned to read referendum questions in advance

Follow for live coverage:

Trump signs memorandum to remove Canadian goods from U.S. procurement

U.S. President Donald Trump signed a presidential memorandum to identify and remove Canadian items from the U.S. federal procurement system, the White House announced Wednesday.

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trump threatened move earlier this month

The move comes one week after Trump posted on Truth Social that he was directing U.S. federal agencies that oversee government procurement to remove all Canadian-origin products from its “awards schedules,” one of many announcements the U.S. president made after Canada imposed its latest set of retaliatory tariffs.

Trump claimed the Canadian items within the award schedules account to “more than 50 BILLION DOLLARS a year.”

“The Canadian Government, including Canadian Provinces, have banned American Small Businesses and Companies from selling into their Government Procurement Markets,” Trump wrote.

“That is not reciprocity, it is a Canadian Trade Scam,” Trump posted. “From now on, NO RECIPROCITY — NO ACCESS!”

Hunter Crowther, CTVNews.ca producer

‘Conservatives say no EU taxes’: Poilievre

Poilievre says although the Conservative party will continue to support co-operation with European allies, they are unhappy with Carney’s ambiguity about a potential alliance.

“We have the longest history of supporting the NATO alliance, which includes 30 European countries. That’s not new,” the party leader told a room full of Conservatives in Penticton, B.C. “The Prime Minister, however. needs to get his story straight.”

As Poilievre called out Carney for “secretly negotiating” a possible associate membership or a unique alliance with the EU, he added that the Conservatives are clear on one thing.

“Conservatives say no EU taxes, no EU laws, and no EU open-border rules on immigration in Canada.”

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Poilievre criticizes Carney during caucus remarks

Poilievre says although he refrained from criticizing Carney during his trip to the United States, he joked that now that he’s on home soil, he’s prepared to “make up for lost time.”

Speaking after the first day of the Conservative caucus retreat in Penticton, B.C., Poilievre told colleagues that “our job is to unite to fight for Canada abroad, at the same time as doing our duty of holding the government accountable here at home. That is what it means to be a loyal Opposition.”

Poilievre went on to criticize Carney for what he described as a failure to deliver results for Canadians at the gas pump, the grocery store and on rent, while planning “summits and speeches and symbolic signing ceremonies.”

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Poilievre: Canada must be independent

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says Carney “can’t seem to get his story straight” about the nature of the deal between Canada and the EU.

Poilievre appears to be poking at the different terminology used by Canadians and Europeans in recent days. He referenced the “associate membership” – as von der Leyen put it today – and “unique alliance” – as Carney said yesterday.

“Conservatives are clear: we support the decades-old free trade & NATO defence alliance with Europe,” wrote the party leader on X.

“But no EU taxes, no EU laws, and no EU open-border immigration policies should be imposed on Canadians. Canada must be independent and sovereign. Period.”

Earlier today, reporters pressed Canada’s ambassador designate to the EU Jonathan Wilkinson on what exactly leaders were negotiating. He said that details of a new relationship between Canada and the EU were still in flux, and that once terms are solidified, they’ll decide what to call it.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Canada seeks full membership in U.K.-led military coalition

Carney says Canada has formally applied to join the U.K.-led Joint Expeditionary Force as a full-time member, a bid that London is supporting.

The joint force is a military coalition made up of 10 NATO allies which was struck in 2014 to create a quick-response force.

Canada’s military has worked with the force in multinational drills but has not been a permanent member of the group.

On Wednesday, Carney met for the first time with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who took office after Keir Starmer resigned over the summer.

Read the full story here

PM Carney, U.K. PM take in soccer match

Carney has arrived in Liverpool where he’ll attend an Everton FC match alongside new U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Both men are fans of the club.

Appearing together before the match, Burnham called Carney a “great progressive leader.”

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

You can read The Associated Press’ full story here

Carney, von der Leyen meet

Carney and von der Leyen discussed “deep co-operation” between Canada and the EU during their meeting today.

That’s according to a readout from the Prime Minister’s Office, which did not include mention of the so-called “associate member” status for Canada.

However, the leaders discussed moving “beyond” their existing trade deal to a “far stronger, more ambitious alliance in the future.”

Areas to expand co-operation include critical minerals, defence, AI, energy, space and “financial services and payments.”

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Trump criticizes Canada over drugs

U.S. President Donald Trump is again accusing Canada of not doing enough to clamp down on drugs but did not include it in a list of major drug-producing countries released today.

The list, which is published each year, cites Afghanistan, China, Colombia, Guatemala, Haiti, Mexico and other nations deemed major drug producers.

In a declaration submitted to Congress, Trump praised the efforts of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum’s administration to stop the flow of drugs and shut down labs but said Mexico and Canada still need to do more.

Trump alleged that fentanyl is being made in clandestine Canadian labs and transported south into the United States, and claimed Chinese gangs are operating along the border.

U.S. government data shows a minuscule volume of drugs is seized at the northern border compared to the boundary with Mexico.

Trump used fentanyl as a reason to hit Canada with tariffs last year before the U.S. Supreme Court struck down those duties.

Kelly Geraldine Malone, The Canadian Press

Canada must ‘stand on our two feet’

Hours before departing for Chicago to meet Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Industry Minister Melanie Joly said Canada is still engaging with U.S. counterparts.

“That being said, we need to stand on our two feet,” she added, speaking alongside Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow in Toronto.

She said she’s looking to align policies with the EU to protect Canada’s aluminum and steel sectors.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

EU group supports Canadian inclusion

Renew Europe, which holds 77 of the 720 seats in the European Parliament, says it supports making Canada an associate member.

“Let’s take our partnership to the next level!” the party wrote on social media.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

What’s in a name?

Ambassador designate to the EU Jonathan Wilkinson says Canada isn’t trying to get ahead of itself when it comes to what to call a Euro-Canuck partnership.

“Eventually, we’ll get to the issue of what’s the best way to describe it,” he said. But membership brings sovereignty concerns, and details of just what Canada would share with the EU is still up for negotiation.

Referring to von der Leyen’s invitation to reach “associate member” status, Wilkinson said, “We’re not there.

“It’s an opportunity for us to talk about that, but we’re really much more focused on getting concrete results.”

“I think we’ve actually got to get to the point where we know what we’re describing,” he also said.

Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist

Ford welcomes airport investment plan

Ontario Premier Doug Ford is voicing his support for a proposal to seek private investors for four Canadian airports, noting that it “should have been done years ago.”

Ford made the comment during a news conference on Wednesday, one day after Prime Minister Mark Carney unveiled his plans during a keynote address in Toronto.

In addition to Toronto’s Pearson airport, the federal government is also opening airports in Montreal, Calgary, and Vancouver to private investment.

“I think it’s fabulous. You know, I have to give credit where credit’s due. The PM’s on fire. He’s moving. He’s lowering taxes like we’ve done for years. He’s privatizing airports that should have been done years ago,” Ford said.

Ford told reporters that he would also like to see Toronto’s Billy Bishop Airport opened to private investment.

In July, a proposal to expand the airport with billions in private investments was blocked by the federal government.

Chris Fox, CTVNewsToronto.ca journalist

Canada already has agreements with EU: Poilievre

Speaking to reporters before the prime minister’s trip to Europe, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Canada already has trade and defence agreements with the EU, in the form of CETA and NATO.

“We want Canada to have free trade with Europe, co-operation with Europe, but we will never surrender our independence and sovereignty over our laws, our tax money, and our immigration policies,” Poilievre said.

He added the Conservatives want to see “an economic action plan” to support Canadians struggling with the cost of living, rather than an unclear goal of potentially conforming to European systems and policies.

Spencer Van Dyk, CTV News writer & producer

Canada, EU share ‘one set of values’

With Carney sitting front row, the president of the European Commission declared to her Parliament that she wants to bring the relationship with Canada “to the highest level possible.”

In her widely watched State of the Union address to the EU Parliament, von der Leyen stated plainly, with Carney seated to her left: “I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU.”

As she said it, many elected officials in the chamber rose from their seats and applauded. Carney got out of his, walked up to her podium, and shook von der Leyen’s hand.

She made this declaration after speaking at length about the challenges Europe is facing and her aspirations for the year ahead.

Von der Leyen also said that at this moment in geopolitics, the EU needs to “urgently reimagine our partnerships,” and that she sees Canada as an ideal country to do that with.

“We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world. And we will now build our shared future as well,” she said.

Rachel Aiello, CTV News correspondent. Read the full story here.

No more ‘love letters’

Since Canada joining the EU as an associate member would be a first, there is no rulebook on how that would work or what it would mean in practice. It is unclear who would need to approve membership, and how long that could take.

Currently, all steps toward EU membership must be approved unanimously by the 27 member countries.

The idea of associate membership has been floated in the past for Ukraine, or for post-Brexit Britain, but no concrete steps have been taken.

The relationship between Canada and the European Union has reached a point where the two sides need to move beyond rhetoric and start building something more substantive, said Tobias Cremer, a German member of the European Parliament.

“Now is the time to stop sending each other love letters and put meat on the bone,” said Cremer, from the centre-left Social Democrats.

He argued that any new arrangement should be more ambitious than another trade or defence agreement, describing the goal as a more holistic strategic alliance between Canada and the EU.

The Associated Press

‘Buy Ontario’ is the law: Ford

Ontario municipalities could face cuts to provincial funding if they fail to comply with “Buy Ontario” procurement rules, warned Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing Rob Flack Wednesday.

In a letter to municipalities, the minister said local governments must maximize the use of Ontario and Canadian goods and services as the province responds to U.S. tariffs and other trade measures.

In practice, municipalities spend more than $22 billion each year on goods and services, and the province says those purchases should prioritize Ontario and Canadian products.

“Failure to comply with Buy Ontario requirements will force us to reconsider provincial funding made available to municipalities, in addition to other consequences under the Buy Ontario Act,” the minister wrote.

Ontario’s Premier Doug Ford also shared the letter to social media Wednesday morning, writing “Buy Ontario. Buy Canadian. For governments across Ontario, it’s not an option. It’s the law.”

Municipalities have been directed to review their supply chains, procurement practices and upcoming purchases to determine whether products and services currently sourced outside Canada can be replaced with domestic alternatives.

Jermaine Wilson, CTVNews.ca & CP24.com journalist

How Canada can appeal to investors

Canada’s move to slash its marginal effective tax rate is just one in a series of steps to make it appealing to investors, according to an expert.

“It’s a terrific concept,” Jay Kosla, executive director of economic and energy policy at the Public Policy Forum told CTV Your Morning on Wednesday. “We’ll have to see how it plays out in reality.”

He said Canada needs to fulfil at least five requirements to entice businesses into bringing in their mega projects.

The first is project financing, he said. The second is an “efficient and effective” regulatory system, which provides certainty to investors.

He listed Indigenous economic participation as the third requirement, and said the fourth and fifth factors are enabling infrastructure and required labour.

“The main point, though, is these projects need a high degree of tactile oversight.”

Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist

Ontario town removes U.S. flag

The decision to remove the American flag in one central Ontario town is sparking discussion about the Canada-U.S. relationship.

Meaford council voted on Monday night to remove the American flag that was flying high in Market Square, right beside Town Hall.

Mayor Ross Kentner tells CTV News it’s the “pressures against our sovereignty” that has citizens angry. “As President [Donald] Trump continued to use and abuse Canadians, people have got their backs up.”

Staff brought the report and recommendation to council, with members voting 5-1 to take down the flag.

  • Meaford council votes to take down American flag from prominent spot

While it wasn’t unanimous, Coun. Harley Greenfield, the sole member who voted against the recommendation, was in favour of bringing down the American flag to half-mast instead.

His reasoning was that it could be a symbol of Canadians grieving the loss of the relationship we had with the U.S.

Jocelyn Martin, CTVNewsBarrie.ca journalist. Read the full story here.

Poilievre must unite party: sources

As he gathers his caucus in B.C. this week, Pierre Poilievre faces a tall order: unite factions and find a way to punch through in Parliament this fall, according to a number of sources who spoke to CTV News.

Federal Conservatives from across the country meet in Penticton Wednesday and Thursday, before heading back to Ottawa later this month.

Speaking to CTV News on background ahead of the retreat, one caucus source described the group as a “fractured mess,” saying many members view the event as a sort of vacation from their ridings, after working hard at home this summer, worried about losing their seats.

The source said up until last fall, caucus largely bought the message that the 2025 election loss and low polling numbers were a “temporary setback.”

But consistently lagging polling and internal division make it “increasingly difficult for caucus to believe the narrative that we’ll be back on top one day,” the source said.

“This is what it looks like when a leader is starting to really lose the room,” said the University of British Columbia’s Stewart Prest, adding that it appears the party is struggling to “gain traction on any major issue.”

Abigail Bimman, CTV News correspondent. Read the full story here.

Separation referendum in Alberta

Albertans preparing to vote in October’s provincial referendum are being encouraged to read the questions ahead of time, after academics identified several examples of wording that can make voters stop, reread and reconsider what they are being asked.

The 10 questions cover issues including immigration, access to provincially funded programs, voting requirements, constitutional reform and Alberta’s relationship with Canada.

Nine are yes-or-no questions, while the 10th asks voters to choose between remaining a province of Canada or beginning the legal process required to hold a future binding referendum on separation.

Elections Alberta says its staff will not be able to explain what any of the questions mean or what the government intended by them at voting locations.

“We’re really encouraging Albertans to read those questions in advance and work to understand those questions in advance before they come into the voting locations,” said Michelle Gurney, a spokesperson for Elections Alberta.

Mark Villani, CTV News Calgary journalist. Read the full story here.

items.body:
UNITED NATIONS — The United Nations chief urged global competitors in artificial intelligence on Wednesday to co-operate in addressing threats from the technology, warning that “the world cannot afford a race to the bottom on AI safety.”

Secretary-General António Guterres said concerns raised by those on the frontlines of AI technology that its development “is racing ahead of our understanding of the risks” can’t be ignored.

Governments must assume their first responsibility to protect civilians from AI threats, which means “national action is essential,” Guterres told UN reporters. “But global coordination is also indispensable.”

“We need guardrails to build trust — and that make AI safe, transparent, accountable, with human dignity at the centre.”

Guterres was referring to a proposal from Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, to ensure AI safety by coordinating a slowdown in its development by leading technology companies and governments.

OpenAI’s Sam Altman, SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk and other prominent industry leaders have said in recent days that AI’s development needs to slow down. But Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg distanced the company Wednesday, saying every AI company has to ensure its technology is safe.

There are other obstacles to a coordinated effort on AI, including domestic and global competition, especially from China, and profit motivations. And there has been pushback from U.S. President Donald Trump, who this week called threats that AI might destroy humanity “a HOAX” and claimed efforts to limit the technology are part of a “SICK conspiracy.”

Guterres has praised the enormous potential of AI, including to accelerate economic development and education and to strengthen health systems. But he has also warned of the “existential” threat of “runaway artificial intelligence.” He said AI will be a major topic in his discussions with world leaders at their annual gathering next week for the high-level session of the UN General Assembly.

“The United Nations will continue to explore practical ideas and approaches in the immediate days ahead,” Guterres said. “We need a shared understanding of how to advance the safe, secure and responsible development of AI — while identifying when increasingly powerful systems may require stronger safeguards, or additional measures to manage potential risks.”

At Guterres’ behest, the General Assembly established the first global scientific body on AI in 2025. In its preliminary report in July, the 40-member panel warned that the rapid, unchecked use of AI at scale risks harm to the mental health of users, “potential use as a destructive tool, impacts on social, economic and environmental systems, and challenges associated with controlling the technology.”

The secretary-general told reporters he is aware that geopolitical divides might pose problems. But he said countries “that have the highest capacity in the frontiers of AI” should establish contact, exchange information and agree on some common guardrails “to avoid this race to the bottom that could lead one day to a gigantic disaster at global level.”

Guterres responded to a question asking whether next week’s meeting of top officials from the UN’s 193 member nations wouldn’t be the perfect opportunity for a summit on curbing the excesses of AI. He said there wasn’t time to properly prepare a meeting.

But he said, “I think it makes full sense at the right moment to have a serious international summit on artificial intelligence.” And at a summit, he said, “it is absolutely essential to have everybody on board” — governments, companies, scientists and civil society — “and I hope that this will be possible.”

Edith M. Lederer, The Associated Press

items._ogDesc: Digital sovereignty took centre stage at a major artificial intelligence conference, with AI leaders discussing avoiding dependence on less reliable states.
items.body:
Digital sovereignty took centre stage at a major artificial intelligence conference Wednesday, with AI leaders saying homegrown build-outs and collaboration among trusted allies are the key to avoiding dependence on less reliable states.

A failure to construct data centres and forge ahead on AI development at home would leave Canada beholden to its neighbours, said Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon.

“If we don’t build it here, we’ve got to buy it from someone else. And if we don’t innovate here, we’ve got to rent it from someone else. And if we don’t make the rules here, we’ve got to follow someone else’s,” he told attendees at the All In conference in Montreal.

But no nation is an island, he noted.

“Sovereignty’s not isolation; it means partnership with shared values.”

Karsten Wildberger, Germany’s digital minister, told the audience that shared standards and oversight are essential to ensuring both safe AI development and cutting-edge technology.

“Nowhere does sovereignty matter more than AI. Few technologies have had such power to change our lives so quickly,” he said.

The remarks came amid renewed fears over the existential threat potentially posed by AI systems after an employee at AI giant Anthropic quit earlier this month, warning that those systems could spiral out of control and destroy humanity.

The comments also landed as concerns flare up around digital sovereignty after U.S. President Donald last month dubbed Lake Ontario instead Lake America — a change that popped up on some online maps in Canada.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

Wildberger said middle powers such as Canada and Germany should channel that angst into action on AI production, since protests from the sidelines would be drowned out.

“We will sit at the table when we have technology to offer that is safe, capable and competitive. My worry is if our contribution is mainly philosophical; it is important, but that’s not enough,” the minister said.

On Wednesday, Canadian research institute Mila and the German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence announced an agreement to cement AI ties between the two countries. The partnership will focus on developing safe AI systems and applications in key industries such as energy.

Canadian AI company Cohere and German startup Aleph Alpha — both among the biggest large language learning model providers outside of the United States and China — also formalized a previously announced merger in a bid to better compete with American AI giants.

The goal of Cohere’s acquisition is partly to lure companies and governments uneasy with reliance on U.S. tech titans for digital services.

“There need to be multiple democracies contributing to this technology. The world is going to diversify for resilience,” said CEO Aidan Gomez.

As to whether American and Chinese firms would agree to international oversight, he that “it’s going to be tough — but the dialogue needs to be opened.”

“A multinational body is a much better solution than just a bunch of islands trying to regulate this themselves,” he said at a conference panel alongside Solomon, Wildberger and Aleph Alpha chief research officer Samuel Weinbach.

In an interview Wednesday afternoon, Solomon conceded that Canadian businesses and governments remain heavily reliant on American tech, including cloud services run by Amazon and Google. American authorities have the right to access the oceans of data stored by those companies, such as health care records. And Canadian startups use a vast array of U.S.-made AI tools daily.

“Our trade is largely with the United States, and for a long time that was the most secure way to do it. And it continues to be our largest trading partner,” Solomon said.

“I’m not building against anyone. I’m building for Canada,” he said, pointing to Bell Canada’s announcement this week that it plans to quadruple the size of a data centre project in Saskatchewan.

The $50-billion move amounts to the largest capital investment in the province’s history, and comes amid a growing backlash against data centres across the country.

Solomon highlighted the Liberal government’s efforts to introduce privacy legislation that aims to give citizens more control over their data and to establish a new regulator with the power to impose fines on corporations. An AI literacy course for all teachers and high school students is also set to launch next week.

Earlier in the day, he and Germany’s digital minister announced $300 million in funding for LawZero, a non-profit AI safety research organization founded by artificial intelligence guru Yoshua Bengio and incubated at Mila.

The flashy advancements of machine learning were on full display at the conference, with the players on hand ranging from Microsoft and Nvidia to Bengio.

Mila sported a “real or fake” kiosk asking passersby to spot the AI-generated images, and showcasing its open-source technology to detect the pixel-level signatures they leave.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

American AI might also featured prominently. Dell invited attendees to step inside a converted shipping container housing its military-grade mobile data centre, decked out with server racks and cooling units and fit for transport in a military plane.

Meanwhile, Aston Martin showed off its Formula One racing car, with Cohere as an AI partner.

Michael Pelosi, the company’s country manager for Canada, warned about the consequences of failing to diversify the AI models that companies deploy.

“If that model is coming from one market or one region and someone has the ability to turn it off, you’re in trouble,” he said at a Montreal fintech conference Tuesday, noting the U.S. administration’s export ban on an Anthropic model through much of the summer.

“Are you at the mercy of someone — not to mention names, maybe a leader down south — saying, ‘No, I don’t want them to have access to this anymore?’”

Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: U.S. stocks slipped after the U.S. Federal Reserve hiked its main interest rate for the first time in three years and suggested more may be ahead.
items.body:
U.S. stocks slipped Wednesday after the U.S. Federal Reserve hiked its main interest rate for the first time in three years and suggested more may be ahead as it tries to get the nation’s high inflation under control.

The S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent after giving up a modest gain from earlier in the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 631 points, or 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was nearly unchanged after edging down by less than 0.1 per cent.

Investors generally prefer lower interest rates because higher rates slow the economy’s growth and undercut prices for stocks and other investments.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

The U.S. stock market initially held onto its modest, early gains after the Fed announced its decision. The short-term pain of a slower economy may be worth it if it starves inflation of its fuel and gets further increases for the cost of living back to the Fed’s 2 per cent target.

But stock prices weakened later in the day as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said repeatedly in a press conference that inflation remains too high and the U.S. economy appears to be strengthening. That could imply the economy is solid enough to withstand more hikes to rates, and other officials at the Fed provided their own forecasts suggesting rates may need to go still higher.

The median Fed official expects the federal funds rate to end this year at 4.1 per cent, according to forecasts published after the central bank’s meeting. That’s up from its current range of 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent following Wednesday’s increase, and it’s up from the median forecast of 3.8 per cent that Fed officials gave three months ago.

Traders, meanwhile, suspect the Fed may go even further. They’re betting on a 38 per cent probability the Fed could hike the federal funds rate to a range of 4.25 per cent to 4.50 per cent by the end of the year, according to data from CME Group.

“Our decision comes at a time when the American economy appears to be strengthening,” Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said in his press conference.

He pointed to solid U.S. hiring trends, corporate profits and investments by businesses. A report on Wednesday morning, meanwhile, showed shoppers spent much more at U.S. retailers last month than economists expected.

“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said. He later added, “Today‘s action starts to show we’re serious about this.”

It’s the first hike by the Fed to interest rates in three years. The central bank had been on pause for months following cuts to rates in 2024 and 2025, even though inflation has consistently remained above the Fed’s 2 per cent target.

President Donald Trump has been lobbying for interest rates to go lower rather than higher.

On Wall Street, bank stocks fell to some of the market’s sharper losses. A slower U.S. economy could mean less demand for loans from them. Banks also get hurt when the gap narrows between short-term interest rates and longer-term ones because the industry makes profit off the difference.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Following the Fed’s announcements, the two-year Treasury yield jumped to 4.74 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Tuesday. It tends to closely follow expectations for what the Fed will do with the federal funds rate.

The yield on the longer-term 10-year Treasury, meanwhile, takes into account expectations for economic growth and inflation years down the line. It had a more modest increase, ticking up to 5.01 per cent from 5.00 per cent late Tuesday.

Huntington Bancshares fell 5.6 per cent, Citizens Financial Group sank 4.8 per cent and JPMorgan Chase slipped 1 per cent.

The largest loss in the S&P 500 came from J.B. Hunt Transport Services, which lost 13.3 per cent. Its chief financial officer told a conference of analysts late Tuesday that it’s facing higher costs and expects its earnings to drop 5 per cent to 10 per cent from the second quarter to the third.

Stocks of oil companies also weighed on the market after the price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 2.7 per cent to US$105.83. It was the first drop of the week for Brent, which has gotten near US$110 in recent days.

  • Latest updates on investing here

Helping to limit the market’s losses were gains for some influential stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry.

Nvidia rose 0.8 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices climbed 1.6 per cent to recover more of their losses from earlier in the week. AI stocks slid worldwide Monday after leaders of the AI industry called for a slowdown in development to address safety issues for humanity.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 33.92 points to 7,551.81. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 631.21 to 51,461.90, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 3.15 to 25,978.42.

In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1.4 per cent for one of the world’s biggest gains.

Inflation is a worldwide problem, and the European Central Bank hiked rates last week to help diminish it.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

This press release is provided by GlobeNewswire and is published as received.

BRANTFORD, Ontario, Sept. 16, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- On Sunday, September 20, Shelby’s will open the doors of its 50th location at 221 Henry Street in Brantford, and the brand is inviting the entire community to join the celebration. The grand opening will feature “Za Fest in Za West,” a free-entry community festival with inflatables, a reptile show, a live caricature artist, games, prizes and more, alongside opening-day offers that include 100 free Shawarma Boutines and 50% off wraps, bowls and signature items.

For a brand that started with a single trailer, it is a milestone worth celebrating.

A Family Recipe That Grew Into a Canadian Favourite

The Shelby’s story began with two friends, Yazan and Yasser, who met in college and bonded over their shared Middle Eastern roots and a deep love for authentic food. In 2015, they began selling their mother’s traditional chicken shawarma from a small food trailer in Lambeth, Ontario.

Word travelled fast, and guests kept coming back for the flavour, freshness and experience. That small trailer sparked a bigger vision: bringing something different to the local food scene. Shelby’s would celebrate the rich traditions of Middle Eastern shawarma while drawing bold inspiration from flavours around the world.

In a little over a decade, that vision has grown into the most popular Canadian shawarma chain, with 50 locations across Ontario and Alberta, more than 8 million social media followers, and partnerships with the Toronto Maple Leafs, Toronto FC and GoodLife Fitness. Throughout that growth, the founding philosophy has remained consistent: honour tradition, make everything fresh, and give every guest something legendary, or as Shawarma Man likes to say ‘somesing beddar’.

“When we started with one trailer in Lambeth, we never imagined we would one day be opening our 50th store,” said Yazan El-Shalabi, co-founder of Shelby’s. “Every location we have opened has been built on the support of the people around it. Reaching this milestone in Brantford, we wanted to say thank you in the best way we know how, by bringing the whole community together.”

A Culture Built on Giving Back

Shelby’s has grown one neighbourhood at a time, and the brand has never lost sight of who made that growth possible. Giving back to every community that has supported Shelby’s is a core part of its culture, and each new location is an opportunity to be more than a restaurant: to be a good neighbour that shows up for the people it serves.

That commitment is at the heart of the Brantford opening. Rather than a traditional ribbon-cutting, Shelby’s has dedicated its 50th-store celebration to the Brantford community, with free entrance for everyone and activities designed for families and guests of all ages.

Thanking Brantford’s Healthcare Heroes

The celebration begins before the new store even opens its doors. On Friday, September 18, Shelby’s will provide 100 free meals to the staff at Brantford General Hospital as a thank-you to the healthcare workers who care for the community every day.

As a tribute to where it all began, the Shelby’s food truck will be on site for the cause. After the first 100 free meals are served, the truck will continue serving healthcare workers at special pricing in support of the hospital’s frontline teams.

“Healthcare workers give so much of themselves to this community, often without a moment’s break,” said Yasser Ali, co-founder of Shelby’s. “Our story started on wheels, so bringing our food truck to Brantford General Hospital to thank the people who keep this city healthy felt like the right way to begin our time here.”

Za Fest in Za West: A Day for the Whole Family

On Sunday, the new Henry Street location will come alive with a community festival running from 12:30 p.m. to 6:00 p.m. Entrance is free, and guests can enjoy inflatables and games, a reptile show, Creative Corners for young artists, a live caricature artist, a photobooth, and Shelby’s giveaways and prizes throughout the afternoon.

Guests will also be among the first to taste Shelby’s in Brantford, with two grand opening offers available in-store:

Whether they are longtime Shelby’s fans or trying it for the very first time, Brantford residents are invited to come hungry, bring the family, and help celebrate a milestone that belongs as much to the community as it does to the brand.

What: Shelby’s Brantford Grand Opening and “Za Fest in Za West” community festival When: Sunday, September 20, 2026. Grand opening from 12:00 p.m. to 9:00 p.m.; festival from 12:30 p.m. to 6:00 p.m. Where: 221 Henry Street, Brantford, ON Admission: Free

Founded in 2015 by friends Yazan and Yasser as a single food trailer in Lambeth, Ontario, Shelby’s is a fusion Middle Eastern fast-casual restaurant brand that celebrates the traditions of shawarma with bold inspiration from flavours around the world. Today, Shelby’s operates 50 plus locations across Ontario and Alberta, where guests can build their shawarma their way with fresh ingredients made in-house.

The Company is also committed to cultivating meaningful strategic and Indigenous partnerships that bring local knowledge, expertise, and participation to the development of projects while creating shared economic benefits. Today’s changes continue the deliberate build-out of a leadership group matched to that strategy, with direct experience in major project development and execution, project finance, carbon capture and storage, regulatory and Indigenous engagement, risk management, and public company governance.

Mr. Andersen has more than 25 years of senior leadership experience in the midstream and energy sectors, with expertise spanning operations, business development, capital markets, mergers and acquisitions, major project development and execution, commercial and customer offtake arrangements, corporate governance and regulatory and stakeholder matters. He previously served as Chief Operating Officer and Senior Vice President of Pembina Pipeline Corporation, where he oversaw the company’s Pipeline Division and its pipeline transportation, terminalling, storage and rail operations across Canada and the United States. With hands-on experience across the energy and CCS industries, the team has the capabilities to identify, structure, de-risk and advance projects from early-stage development through to investment and execution.

Jackson, Chief Executive Officer. “With Ivy, Rob and Matt on the executive team and a renewed Board, we are confident we have the complete team in place to execute our strategy. On behalf of the Company, I thank Sheila for her leadership as Chair through a period of significant change, and Larry for his years of service.”

Cielo Waste Solutions Corp. is a clean fuels project development company advancing sustainable aviation fuel and other low-carbon energy projects across North America. Cielo combines strategic feedstock partnerships with proven third-party technologies to develop a scalable pipeline of waste-to-fuels projects, anchored by its flagship Project Nahoonai in Prince George, British Columbia.

items.description: The union representing Canadian workers at Stellantis is urging Ottawa to intervene as the automaker looks to sell its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant.

items._ogDesc: The union representing Canadian workers at Stellantis is urging Ottawa to intervene as the automaker looks to sell its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant.
items.body:
The union representing Canadian workers at Stellantis is urging the federal government to intervene as the automaker looks to sell its idled Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to Canadian armoured ⁠vehicle maker Roshel.

In a letter to Industry Minister Mélanie Joly on Wednesday, Unifor national president Lana Payne warned that if Stellantis is successful in selling the facility, the company will have “abandoned” vehicle production at the plant. That would leave more than 2,000 employees out of work and affect suppliers employing thousands nearby, she said.

“There is no comparable economic replacement for this work. Canada’s economy will be worse-off as a result,” Payne wrote.

“It is incumbent on the federal government to do everything possible to prevent this outcome.”

  • Latest updates on company news here

Last Friday, Stellantis said it had signed a memorandum of understanding with Roshel on a potential sale of the Brampton facility. The future of the plant has been a central issue in collective bargaining negotiations between Unifor and Stellantis, which kicked off earlier this month.

But the union said Friday, which it had set as its internal deadline to reach a new tentative deal, that the two sides were at an impasse. The current collective agreement is set to expire Sept. 20 at 11:59 p.m.

Workers at the Brampton plant were laid off when the company halted operations there in 2023.

Last month, the union said it received notice that Stellantis was considering the closure and sale of the plant. The facility had been slated to be retooled for Jeep production, a process that began early in 2024, before the company paused the plan in early 2025.

It later announced it was moving production of the Jeep Compass to the U.S., in what the union has called a violation of its current collective agreement, leaving the plant idled indefinitely.

In her letter to the federal minister, Payne pointed out that when Stellantis relocated Jeep Compass production, it publicly committed to plans for the Brampton plant that would be subject to discussions with the Canadian government.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

She asked Joly to clarify what role Ottawa might’ve played in discussions around the site’s potential sale, and whether the MOU could have breached conditions of the commitment the automaker made to the government.

Speaking to reporters in Toronto on Wednesday, Joly encouraged Unifor and Stellantis to continue negotiations, which she acknowledged have been “difficult and bumpy” to this point.

“When it comes to any potential sale of the plant to any other company, we will make sure that we protect Canadian workers,” the minister said.

“At the end of the day … we want a new model from Stellantis at the Stellantis plant, and we’ll put maximum pressure to make that happen, and if they don’t, we’ll get our money back.”

But Payne said recent developments have complicated the path toward reaching a new collective agreement with the automaker, calling a potential sale of the Brampton plant “a disaster-scenario for the Canadian auto industry and the broader industrial economy.”

“The Stellantis proposal to sell the plant to a non-automaker never should have been considered in the first place and should be met with fierce resistance from the federal government,” Payne wrote.

Stellantis did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Stellantis Canada chairman, president and CEO Trevor Longley said last week the company considered multiple options for the facility and believes Roshel represents “a strong path to restoring sustainable operations” while preserving the site’s manufacturing capabilities.

  • Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.ca

Roshel CEO Roman Shimonov said the company plans to establish a Canadian Centre of Excellence for Defence Manufacturing in Brampton, “in addition to its current automotive production.”

“We are ready to provide letters of commitment for first consideration to laid-off Unifor workers and bring them back to work as early as 2026 through the federal government’s Light Utility Vehicles procurement program and other automotive and defence opportunities,” Shimonov said in a statement last week.

“We look forward to successfully concluding our discussions with Stellantis and implementing our plans to bring over 2,000 jobs, as well as new sovereign capabilities, including the production of ballistic steel, to Canada and to this facility.”

On Wednesday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he agreed with Joly that a “new model” is needed for the plant.

“The province has not given Stellantis a penny for the Brampton facility, but in saying that, we want to work with them,” he said at an unrelated news conference.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

items.title: ‘We’re losing control,’ Canadian AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio warns
items.description: The Canadian computer scientist considered one of the founders of AI, Yoshua Bengio, told AFP that humanity is “losing control” of the technology and that the world needs guardrails similar to nuclear arms controls.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Professor of computer science Yoshua Bengio poses during an interview in Quebec City on May 1, 2024. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Jacques Boissinot]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: The Canadian computer scientist considered one of the founders of AI, Yoshua Bengio, told AFP that humanity is “losing control” of the technology and that the world needs guardrails similar to nuclear arms controls.
items.body:
The Canadian computer scientist considered one of the founders of AI, Yoshua Bengio, told AFP that humanity is “losing control” of the technology and that the world needs guardrails similar to nuclear arms controls.

Fears about the dangers of AI have intensified in recent weeks, as workers from major companies have resigned with warnings about potentially existential threats to human life if the pace of technological advancement is not checked.

Bengio is a University of Montreal professor who won the 2018 Turing Award, computing’s Nobel, alongside Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the “godfather of AI.”

For Bengio, “there’s a reason that companies are saying this is going too fast, that we’re losing control.”

“People like me have been expecting this for a long time,” the 62-year-old told AFP on Tuesday, saying security discussions surrounding AI have not been adequately robust.

There was broad-based alarm after OpenAI disclosed that a swarm of AI agents -- programs that can take actions on their own -- had carried out an unauthorized breach of the open-source platform Hugging Face in July.

Such autonomous action is the central threat, Bengio said, warning of a situation where AI agents “have the ability to get through cybersecurity barriers and enter any company.”

Manipulating human behavior

Last year, Bengio founded the non-profit LawZero, aimed at creating a new form of advanced AI that is “designed to be trustworthy and safe.”

LawZero was awarded $300 million in funding on Wednesday, split jointly between the governments of Canada and Germany, which have launched several efforts to cooperate on AI.

Speaking to AFP a day before the announcement, Bengio said people need to be aware of the risks ahead.

AI agents may foster “an ability to establish an individual connection and persuade humans to act in ways that suit it but are not necessarily good for all of us,” a capability that could have sweeping consequences for democracies, he said.

Longer-term, “AI might not even need human beings anymore to do real things in the physical world,” he added.

In that scenario, “one extreme could be the destruction of humanity,” he warned.

“That’s an extreme,” he acknowledged, but noted that even if a banking system were shut down, “that’s still very, very serious.”

International challenge

The world’s biggest AI companies -- OpenAI, Anthropic and Google -- have begun working on creating a standards body, a collaboration that seemed to acknowledge the public’s fear that competition between companies and countries might sideline safety.

For Bengio, taming AI’s advance is “an international challenge, a bit like nuclear weapons are an international challenge.”

“So the international community needs to understand the power we are bringing into the world, and that must be managed, must be governed through institutions, treaties, and democratic safeguards.”

“Society needs time to put in place what needs to be put in place,” Bengio said.

But political will across key governments appears uneven.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday dismissed warnings about the risks of AI as “hoaxes.”

But there is more openness to act in the EU, where European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday that she will invite the world’s largest AI labs for talks on “how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was at that speech in Strasbourg, has talked repeatedly about collaborating with the EU on AI safety.

Bengio stressed that all firms must comply with future AI restrictions, particularly U.S.-based companies that have so far been dominating the sector.

Action is urgent, he said, but voiced optimism that “we can help bring the world to a place that is more aligned with democratic values and values of power sharing.”

items.title: AI risks wider gender inequality in jobs market: WEF
items.description: The rise of artificial intelligence could exacerbate gender disparities in the labour market, the World Economic Forum and LinkedIn warned.

items._ogDesc: The rise of artificial intelligence could exacerbate gender disparities in the labour market, the World Economic Forum and LinkedIn warned.
items.body:
LONDON, United Kingdom — The rise of artificial intelligence could exacerbate gender disparities in the labour market, the World Economic Forum and careers platform LinkedIn warned in a joint report Wednesday.

“What we found is that the type of roles that are being disrupted by AI tend to be the type of roles that women have been concentrated in,” Saadia Zahidi, a managing board member at the World Economic Forum, told a London gathering for the launch of the Global Gender Gap Report 2026.

“It is white-collar work that has brought in a lot of women and given them very good livelihoods over the last few decades, and here is exactly those roles that are being disrupted,” she added.

Within AI companies, the picture is even more striking, with women significantly less represented than in comparable non-AI companies -- at all levels -- according to the report.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

“Women hold just one in every five AI engineering roles,” Sue Duke, managing director at LinkedIn, told the event.

Without more women in scientific fields and emerging AI roles, the economic opportunities created by this technology could primarily benefit men, suggested Duke, based on the report’s findings.

To avoid widening inequalities, Duke believes it is crucial for governments and businesses to invest in bringing women into AI training pathways and roles from the outset -- and to continue investing at every stage of their careers.

While gender disparities have narrowed worldwide since the first such WEF report was published 20 years ago, its latest data shows the trend towards closing the inequality gap has slowed in the last decade compared with the previous ten years.

items._ogDesc: Cheaper mortgage financing barely begun to help the real estate recovery but it’s already set to disappear, warns BMO Capital Markets.
items.body:
Canada’s real estate recovery has barely begun but it already faces headwinds. Rising inflation and credit demand has the market now expecting 5 rate hikes. This morning, BMO Capital Markets told investors that 5 hikes seems a little much right now. However, the bank warned that rates will rise and mortgage relief for this cycle is over.

Investors Expect Interest Rates To Climb Sharply

The pressure on higher interest rates is clear. Headline CPI’s annual growth sits at 3.0%, the upper limit of tolerance for the Bank of Canada (BoC). Bond yields have responded, with the 5-year government bond adding 10 basis points (bps) in the past 5 days. It’s climbed 51 bps over the past 3 months, though consumer borrowing costs have yet to show the change. Experts also see higher costs rolling in over the next few weeks.

The market sees the current 2.25% overnight rate adding another 125 bps, or 1.25 percentage points. That works out to roughly 5 hikes, pushing the overnight rate to 3.5% by the end of 2027. Higher rates are bad news for the Canadian real estate market, which has been at a standstill for years. Especially with prices still well out of reach for the average household.

Canadian Real Estate Recovery Already Losing Steam As Sales Stall

Canadian real estate markets may have diverged when it comes to prices, but sales are slow all around. Coming in just slightly weaker than last year, some economists are now calling the bottom. That may be true, but the bottom for sales doesn’t necessarily indicate a recovery is around the corner.

“Canada’s housing market has been stable through the summer, and conditions remain balanced at the national level,” explains BMO senior economist Robert Kavcic. “Volumes and prices continue to carve out bottoms in the hardest-hit markets, but the recovery is going to be flat with little in the pipeline to trigger a sharp rebound.”

The bank sees rising rates putting a cap on demand and higher prices over the near-term. But it also thinks the market is overestimating the number of rate hikes.

Canadian Mortgage Rates Expected To Rise Soon

Source: BMO Capital Markets.

BMO previously warned that upward pressure on rates would cool the market. Affordabilty levers such as cheap credit and higher incomes have already been exhausted. They see lower prices as the only path forward to revive market activity. Kavcic reiterated the bank’s position that rising yields will kill fixed-rate relief.

“Higher longer-term bond yields and, therefore, fixed mortgage rates will continue to dampen the recovery and push many buyers into variable rates,” warns Kavcic.

Those trying to move to a variable rate to save from the lag may not find relief for long. The bank may see fewer hikes in their forecast, but they do see rate hikes ahead.

“We believe that [100 bps] is too aggressive, but it certainly looks like we’ve seen all the mortgage rate relief that we will see for this stage of the cycle—and that will keep any housing rebound well in check,” says Kavcic.

BMO is far from the only bank that’s warning investors that housing is reentering choppy waters. National Bank economists warned that mortgage rates will be climbing with yields soon. Its analysis found lenders are absorbing higher yields with narrower spreads. While that works short-term to drum up business, it’s not a sustainable path according to the bank. items.description: Exploratory EU mobility talks raise employment and compliance questions for Canadian HR teams
items.content: <p>Exploratory EU mobility talks raise employment and compliance questions for Canadian HR teams</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/036/0363_639251472664498753.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Exploratory EU mobility talks raise employment and compliance questions for Canadian HR teams
items.body:
Canadian HR professionals may be interested in recent discussion between Prime Minister Mark Carney and leaders of the European Union (EU) as it could lead to visa-free relocation for Canadians.

Carney has raised the idea of visa-free settlement for Canadians with EU leaders, most often with French President Emmanuel Macron, according to two officials cited by the Wall Street Journal, cited by IMI Daily.

The report described the talks as part of a broader push toward "associate member" status for Canada, a category that does not currently exist in EU frameworks. 

Speaking to reporters at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), Carney said "We're not looking to become a member of the European Union," calling the goal instead "a unique alliance between Canada and the European Union" built on shared values, reported IMI Daily.

Global mobility planning

Freedom of movement inside the EU and European Economic Area (EEA) is tied to citizenship, not residency, so any deal would affect Canadian passport holders before permanent residents. That distinction matters for global mobility planning, a topic Canadian HR Reporter has explored in coverage of whether immigration can offset the country's aging workforce.

Serhan Aysever, managing partner at Beyond Global Partners in the United Kingdom, said broader mobility rights would "significantly enhance the value of the Canadian passport," making citizenship "even more attractive to internationally mobile families and investors," according to the IMI Daily report.

He was equally clear on the difficulty involved, describing any framework as "a significant policy shift around free movement, residence and employment rights for a non-EU country" and "a serious and potentially lengthy policy process" that would take years to negotiate, according to the article.

'Highly speculative' 

Charlie Maggi, founder and CEO of The Open World in France, called the reports "politically significant, but still highly speculative." A narrow, sector-specific deal looks more likely to him than universal access across all industries, according to IMI Daily.

"Some Canadians, particularly in strategic sectors, could eventually be allowed to live and work in the EU," Maggi said, though full access for all citizens "seems unlikely in the short term," tempering expectations for near-term change, according to the report.

Carney addresses the European Parliament in Strasbourg between Sept. 15 and 17, 2026, ahead of a Canada-EU Summit in Ottawa on Oct. 29 and 30, 2026. 

According to a previous study, a clear majority of Canadian citizens think joining the EU is either good or at least worth exploring. 

One of the EU’s core attractions is its single-market model, where people can move and work freely, Amy Verdun, professor of comparative politics at the University of Victoria, previously told Canadian HR Reporter.

"They would have free movement of labour, so it means that anybody anywhere in the EU would have the equivalent of a right to work in Canada, as if they were a Canadian citizen.”

A newly-constructed “best-in-class” industrial property in Mississauga has hit the market, according to a listing that came online earlier this month.

Owned by CanFirst Capital Management, the property is located at 6525 Mississauga Road on the northeast corner of the intersection with Turner Valley Road in the Meadowvale area of Mississauga.

Directly to the north are two warehouses that are both home to Walmart Canada, and across the street to the west is the five-building Meadowvale Corporate Centre that transacted in late-2024, as previously reported by STOREYS.

6525 Mississauga Road is a 14.08-acre property, home to a warehouse and distribution facility that was constructed in 2024 and spans 270,738 sq. ft. According to CanFirst, concrete from the previous building was demolished on site and re-used beneath the slab of the new building, and 30% of the materials used met sustainable sourcing criteria.

The facility is 100% leased to telecommunications giant TELUS (TSX: T) with approximately 10.5 years remaining on the lease term. The lease features contractual annual rent escalations, with two five-year renewal options at fair market rent, providing stable cash flows and an investment-grade tenant.

6525 Mississauga Road and its surrounding context. (RBC Capital Markets & CBRE)

The Listing

6525 Mississauga Road was listed for sale earlier this month on an unpriced basis by David Tweedie, Tim Pacaud, and Keith Chan of RBC Capital Markets Realty, alongside Scott Mackenzie, Jordan Lunan, and Brett Thorne of CBRE.

  • Address: 6525 Mississauga Road, Mississauga, Ontario
  • Year Built: 2024
  • Site Area: 14.08 acres
  • Existing Leasable Area: 270,738 sq. ft
  • Current Occupancy Rate: 100%
  • Price: Unpriced
  • Listed By: RBC Capital Markets Realty (David Tweedie, Tim Pacaud, and Keith Chan) and CBRE (Scott Mackenzie, Jordan Lunan, and Brett Thorne)

Property details for 6525 Mississauga Road. (RBC Capital Markets & CBRE)

From a location standpoint, the property is also just one-kilometre south of the Highway 401 interchange, with good proximity to two GO transit stations — Meadowville GO and Lisgar GO — as well as Toronto Pearson International Airport.

According to RBC and CBRE, Mississauga’s availability rate for Class A industrial space was at 0.7% as of Q2 2026, with average net asking rents in the area commanding a premium over the Greater Toronto Area, resulting in a favourable outlook for well-located and high-quality assets.

“The offering presents investors with a rare opportunity to acquire a newly constructed, 100% leased institutional-quality industrial asset, combining long-term carefree net lease cash flow with contractual rent growth secured by one of Canada’s most creditworthy corporate tenants, in the GTA’s premier industrial corridor.”

items._ogDesc: Acquisition expands Concord’s renewable energy pipeline to more than one gigawatt of capacity across Canada
items.body:
Concord Pacific is expanding its renewable energy business with the acquisition of a major wind project in Saskatchewan.

Concord Green Energy, the renewable energy division of Vancouver-based Concord Pacific, has acquired the Golden South Wind Project near Assiniboia, Sask.

The utility-scale facility has 50 wind turbines with 210 megawatts of installed generation capacity and 200 megawatts of contracted capacity. It generates enough electricity to meet the annual needs of up to 100,000 homes, according to a Concord announcement Monday.

“Golden South represents an important step in growing Concord Green Energy into a larger Canadian renewable energy business,” said Terry Hui, president and CEO of Concord Pacific Group.

“Canada is entering a period of significant investment in the power and infrastructure needed to support economic growth, and the federal government’s renewed focus on green, reliable energy creates a strong environment for long-term investment.”

With the acquisition, Concord Green Energy’s operating portfolio grows to about 543 megawatts of installed renewable generation capacity.

The company said its operating assets and projects under development now represent more than one gigawatt of renewable energy capacity across Canada. Its portfolio includes wind, solar, hydroelectric generation and energy storage projects.

Golden South was previously owned by Toronto-based Potentia Renewables Inc., which will continue to manage the project’s day-to-day operations following the acquisition.

The project began commercial operations in March 2022 and operates under a 25-year power purchase agreement with SaskPower, Saskatchewan's main supplier of electricity.

items._ogDesc: Canadian real estate prices fell for a 3rd month in August, as weak sales and sticky inventory pushed the demand balance to a 29-year low.
items.body:
Canadian real estate’s recovery hit pause last month—and maybe even rewound a bit. Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data shows that home prices slipped in August. Weak sales, sticky inventory, and economic uncertainty have led to the weakest demand balance in nearly 30 years.

Canadian Real Estate Prices Fall For A Third Month

The price of a typical home across Canada.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

The price of a typical home slipped 0.7% (-$4.3k) to $657,500 in August, marking a third month lower. Prices are now 3.0% (-$20.4k) lower than last year and sit 21.8% (-$183.6k) below the March 2022 peak. Prices are now back to where they were in January of this year, roughly the same as they were back in February 2021.

Canadian Home Sales Just Had The Weakest August Since 2012

Non-seasonally adjusted home sales through the MLS in August.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Existing home sales slipped 6.9% from last year to 37,504 units in August. It wouldn’t be a particularly noteworthy drop on its own, but sales were already weak. The compounding erosion has led to the weakest August since 2012.

Canadians Are Still Listing Homes For Sale In Record Volumes

New listings of homes for sale on the MLS in August.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

Sellers are still out in full force, though there was a small pullback in the volume. CREA reported 74,028 new listings in August, 3.2% lower than last year. It was still the second-highest volume for August since 2020, and the third-highest in at least 20 years of data. New listings might have slipped lower, but inventory is still at one of the highest levels on record.

Canadian Real Estate Demand Balance Falls To 29-Year Low

The sales to new listings ratio (SNLR) for August.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

The board reported a SNLR of 50.7% in August, down 2 points from last year and a big change from the 76.9% at the August 2021 peak. In a local market, this would be considered a balanced reading where buyer and seller demand are equal. Averaged across the country, the meaning is less clear and needs some context. Last month’s SNLR was the weakest for August since 1997, nearing a generational low.

Home buying remains unusually weak and inventory remains lofty—it’s easy to see why. Buyers are already jittery in this environment, and economic uncertainty due to trade war escalation isn’t helping. Add to that upward pressure on financing costs, which at least one bank expects to push prices lower.

items.title: What this week’s bond market chaos could mean for Canadian mortgages
items.description: Fixed rates are soaring, with new doubts about the Bank of Canada’s next steps. What’s in store for the mortgage market?
items.content: <p>Fixed rates are soaring, with new doubts about the Bank of Canada’s next steps. What’s in store for the mortgage market?</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639250880289419422.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Fixed rates are soaring, with new doubts about the Bank of Canada’s next steps. What’s in store for the mortgage market?
items.body:
Global bond market jitters are sending yields higher, with the US 10-year Treasury yield climbing on Monday to a level not seen since 2007. In Canada, the five-year yield is also surging – putting upward pressure on fixed mortgage rates and potentially casting doubt on the housing market outlook for the rest of the year.

Lenders have scrambled to adjust fixed rates amid that rise, which has seen the five-year yield spike by about 90 basis points from where it lay at the same time last year.

The reasons for the bond market unease range from geopolitical chaos to soaring oil prices as the US-Iran war continues, fuelling fears that higher costs will spill into inflation and potentially push central banks into raising interest rates.

The worsening rate outlook is looming large for homebuyers and owners as the fall market comes into view, according to Toronto-based Tango Financial mortgage agent and realtor Victor Tran (pictured top).

“Fixed mortgage rates have been climbing and now the forecasts for the prime rate will probably [rise] – because it’s not looking too good,” Tran told Canadian Mortgage Professional. “It’s likely going to be increasing sooner than we expected.

“It’s all tied to the ongoing tension and trade war with the US. So that’s certainly starting off the fall slower than expected. Typically, the spring market is the best time to sell and then the fall market is the second best, but it’s definitely starting from a slower pace.”

Canada’s housing market faces yet another challenge

That oil price volatility has clouded the Canadian housing outlook since the end of February, while the beginning of a potentially punishing US-Canada trade war in August may also have given some prospective homebuyers pause as they weigh a move.

The recent rise in bond yields and borrowing costs marks just the latest twist for buyers and could move a hoped-for housing recovery even further back.

“Just in the past less than two weeks, the five-year government bond yield increased by 40 basis points. That’s a huge increase in a short amount of time,” Tran said. “The buyers that had rates locked in before the rate hike might feel some pressure into finding something just so they can secure the rate.

“But it’s tough in certain markets where there’s bidding wars in a lot of desirable areas. The buyers that are looking for condos – they have a little bit more breathing room. There’s not as much pressure, there’s still some supply out there. But the rising bond yields and rising fixed mortgage rates definitely kind of throws a wrench in things.”

Could central bank rate hikes be ahead?

In the US, soaring Treasury yields and inflation concerns have seen traders rapidly up their expectations of a rate hike in tomorrow’s announcement by the Federal Reserve.

The Bank of Canada has stayed on hold this year and is still expected to keep rate hikes on ice in its next decision, scheduled for October 28. Still, economists see a growing chance of an increase in December if oil prices continue to rise – possibly spelling bad news for variable-rate mortgage holders and shoppers who could see their rates jump.

“The variable-rate forecast isn’t looking too good either,” Tran said. “So we have people sitting in variable rates considering locking into fixed rates, for example.”

That’s not to say a deep freeze is necessarily ahead. Potential homebuyers have been dealing with dramatic headlines for years, and Tran said many will decide to push ahead with their move despite the wider turbulence.

“It’s really hard to plan for these things. I think a lot of buyers are kind of just tired, especially buyers that have been waiting to purchase a home and that have been in the market for a little while,” he said.

“I think regardless of what happens in the market, they will still move forward with the purchase. Because time goes on. Life moves on. You can only wait for so long for certain opportunities.”

items._ogDesc: What Canada's top brokers are learning, doing, and debating next week in Toronto
items.body:
Canada's largest mortgage industry event opens its doors at the International Centre in Toronto on September 23 and 24, bringing together more than 2,000 brokers, lenders, executives, and technology innovators for two days of sessions built around the pressures defining the Canadian mortgage market this year.

The event — an evolution of the former Canadian Mortgage Summit — arrives at a moment when the industry is navigating its biggest renewal cycle in recent memory.

Canadian residential mortgage debt has reached $2.3 trillion, the broker channel now commands a 33% market share, and 2026 is set to be the largest renewal year in recent history, with 1.15 million mortgages coming up for renewal.

Against that backdrop, organisers have structured the two-day programme around hard, practical content across two concurrent stages.

Attendance is free. Registration is available at mortgagefest.ca.

What's on at MortgageFest Canada

Day One opens with a keynote from Derek Burleton, vice president and deputy chief economist at TD Bank Group, who will map rate and housing activity through the next 24 months.

A Summit Stage panel featuring senior representatives from TD Bank, BMO BrokerEdge, First National Financial LP, and National Bank will follow, examining where prime lenders are currently approving deals, where they are pulling back, and how deal structure affects approval speed and outcomes.

Two AI-focused sessions feature prominently across both days. On Day One, Dalia Barsoum, co-founder and chief executive of Wisely AI Technologies and founder of Streetwise Mortgages in Canada, walks through real workflows her brokerage has built across the full mortgage lifecycle, from lead management to renewals.

On Day Two, a panel featuring Tracey Robinson of Finastra examines where AI is already shifting deal flow and where human judgment stays essential. 

Joe White, founder and chief executive of REMIC, will present a session on Day One drawing on a national survey of 1,910 Canadians, examining how many are already turning to AI for mortgage advice, and the compliance exposure that creates for licensed professionals.

Discover how an award-winning brokerage is using AI across lead management, underwriting support, compliance, marketing, and renewals, while keeping human expertise at the center of the process at #MortgageFest Canada!

Register: https://t.co/qK68QcxmrQ pic.twitter.com/Ji1k0CxI5k — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) September 11, 2026

The renewal wave and AI in the broker channel

The Insights Stage, running parallel to the Summit Stage across both days, is designed around interactive broker-led formats.

Sessions cover tax structuring, lead generation, compliance, and succession, with each session structured to deliver a concrete takeaway — a checklist, a framework, or a decision — rather than a traditional presentation format.

The afternoon programme on Day One includes a panel on alternative lending featuring senior figures from WealthONE Bank of Canada, EQ Bank, Haventree Bank, and MCAN Financial.

A closing spotlight session will bring together prominent brokers Ron Butler of Butler Mortgage Inc., Vince Gaetano of OwlMortgage Inc., and Tracy Valko of Valko Financial Ltd. and DLC AIMI Mortgage Collective Group to share where they see the market heading into the final quarter of 2026.

Day Two opens with a keynote from Jessica Holmes, a comedian and motivational speaker who has shared stages with Ellen DeGeneres, Jerry Seinfeld, and Oprah Winfrey, and who will address resilience in a high-pressure market environment.

Sessions on Day Two include a panel on private and mortgage investment corporation (MIC) lending, a session on serving new-to-Canada borrowers, and a Tech Talk on file efficiency, led by Swish Goswami, chief executive and co-founder of BrokerPlus, walking through how brokers are cutting submission time significantly.

A session from Lindsay Zwart, director of mortgage and housing solutions at Equifax Canada, will also walk brokers through the new 2026 credit report format and its implications for underwriting.

Women in Mortgage Summit Canada

Running alongside Day Two is the Women in Mortgage Summit Canada, a dedicated one-day event bringing together more than 500 women across the industry.

Three Power Panels run across the day, each built around challenges the mortgage community identified as most pressing for 2026, including rate uncertainty, the renewal wave reshaping client books, and buyer hesitation.

Speakers include Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres; Michele Steko, vice president of national broker relations at Sherwood Mortgage Group; and Elena Robinson, vice president of residential sales at First National. 

The event has been pre-approved by Mortgage Professionals Canada for a total of 6.5 continuing education (CE) units in the Professional Development Category and 0.50 CE units in the Compulsory Category for 2026.
